summary: The talk describes the architecture, evaluation, and production deployment of an AI chess coach inside Play Magnus, Magnus Carlsen's consumer chess app. After a game, users receive an AI-powered game review with move-by-move commentary, move quality indicators, and personalized insights about accuracy, rating, and opening depth. The presenters trace chess AI history from Claude Shannon's 1949 type A/type B engine distinction, through Deep Blue's 1997 victory over Kasparov, to DeepMind's AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and finally to LLMs—which hallucinate when asked to play chess directly because they are trained on language, not calculation. The solution pipeline runs Stockfish across the full game for ground-truth best moves, then extracts rich context through tactical and positional detectors (forks, pins, skewers, doubled pawns, structural weaknesses). A novel engine called Maya, built by the University of Toronto, predicts the probability distribution of human moves at given rating levels, letting the system distinguish moves that are best from moves that are also hard to find. All structured signals are fed to the LLM whose sole job is translation into English, minimizing hallucination. For quality assurance, the team maintains 16 eval scenarios covering tactical patterns, blunders, and hallucination limits, using LLM-as-judge and Open Router for rapid model swapping. Gemini Flash passes approximately 75% of scenarios, Claude with extended thinking reaches about 60% with longer latency, and GPT-5 mini shows lower accuracy. The presenters, both strong chess players, provide final quality judgment by comparing their own analysis to the LLM output. For continuous improvement, user-flagged bad commentary posts to Slack and injects into a running Claude Code session via Channels, a new MCP research-preview feature, where Claude autonomously investigates, modifies prompts or detectors, regenerates commentary, asks clarifying questions through Slack, and submits PRs. Key learnings include separating data pipelines from language generation, building a clear context extraction model by iteratively pruning a large JSON structure, closing feedback loops with autonomous agents, and partnering with domain experts for evaluation. End-to-end latency averages about 3 seconds using Gemini 3 Flash at roughly one-second time to first token. A planned 'chat with your coach' feature will accommodate longer-latency reasoning models where users are more patient.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Keeping the LLM as a translator of structured chess signals rather than a reasoner is the core design principle that prevents hallucination.
Stockfish provides ground-truth evaluation; tactical and positional detectors extract teachable concepts; Maya predicts human move probability by rating; the LLM only renders these into English.

16 eval scenarios test tactical patterns, blunders, and hallucination limits; LLM-as-judge and Open Router enable rapid model comparison (Gemini Flash ~75%, Claude with thinking ~60%, GPT-5 mini lower).

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves as Play Magnus employees and outline the agenda: what they built, chess and AI history, why LLMs are bad at chess, their pipeline, agent feedback loop with demo, latency vs quality, and learnings.

sections.title: Play Magnus App and Game Review
sections.summary: Play Magnus is an iOS/Android app for playing chess and sharing games. After each game, users receive an AI-powered game review with move quality indicators and nuanced commentary explaining tactics, threats, and positional concepts. A newer insights layer provides accuracy by phase, rating, and opening depth.

sections.title: Brief History of Chess and AI
sections.summary: Traces from Shannon's 1949 type A (brute force) vs type B (intuitive) engine distinction, through scaling of type A engines leading to Deep Blue's 1997 win over Kasparov, to DeepMind's AlphaGo and AlphaZero which revived type B intuitive neural-network approaches for Go, chess, and shogi.

sections.title: Why LLMs Are Bad at Chess
sections.summary: LLMs sometimes play reasonable openings but quickly hallucinate because they are trained on language, not calculation. DeepMind trained a transformer to predict Stockfish evaluations at grandmaster strength, but such models cannot explain chess in natural language, motivating the need to bridge engines and LLMs.

sections.title: Game Review Pipeline
sections.summary: Pipeline: Stockfish runs through the full game for best moves; tactical and positional detectors extract forks, pins, skewers, doubled pawns, and structural themes; Maya (University of Toronto) predicts human move probability by rating to assess move difficulty. All structured signals feed the LLM whose only job is translation into English to avoid hallucination. Example commentary for an F5 bad move is shown.

sections.title: Closing the Feedback Loop with Agents
sections.summary: User-flagged bad commentary posts to Slack and injects into a running Claude Code session via Channels, a new MCP research-preview feature. Claude runs a commentary triage skill, can modify prompts or detectors, create new detectors, regenerate and verify commentary, ask clarifying questions through Slack, and submit a PR that engineers review and merge from mobile.

sections.title: Live Demo of Feedback Loop
sections.summary: Presenter opens the app on his phone, reports a comment as bad, and the audience sees it post to Slack and inject into the Claude Code channel which invokes the commentary triage skill. Because high-effort runs take a while, they move on and plan to return.

sections.title: Latency vs Quality Trade-offs
sections.summary: Consumer users expect near-instant analysis after a game. The target is sub-3-second commentary generation, achieved with Gemini 3 Flash at roughly one-second time to first token.

sections.title: Evals and Model Comparison
sections.summary: End-to-end latency averages about 3 seconds. Reasoning models produce good quality but have unpredictable latency; a planned 'chat with your coach' feature will accommodate longer waits. The team maintains 16 eval scenarios covering tactical patterns, blunders, and hallucination limits, extracted from real games. They use LLM-as-judge and Open Router to quickly swap models. Gemini Flash passes ~75% of scenarios, Claude with extended thinking ~60% with longer latency, and GPT-5 mini shows lower accuracy. The presenters, both strong chess players, provide final quality judgment by comparing their own analysis to the LLM output.

sections.title: Learnings and Best Practices
sections.summary: Key learnings for practitioners: separate the data pipeline from language generation for low-latency applications; close the feedback loop with autonomous agents; build a clear context extraction model by starting with a large JSON and iteratively pruning to improve quality; and use automated evals with domain experts who may be different from the builders. The presenters also announce a chess simul event at 3:45 p.m. with wooden chess board prizes.

sections.title: Demo Return and Close
sections.summary: Returning to the Claude Code demo, it is still processing. It has added a comment investigating the position and asks via Slack what specifically feels wrong about the commentary. The presenters realize the commentary was actually correct—nothing was wrong—demonstrating that the feedback loop can validate existing quality as well as catch issues.

demonstrations: Live demo: presenter opens the Play Magnus app on his phone, navigates to a game comment, reports it as bad, and the event posts to Slack and injects into a running Claude Code channel that invokes the commentary triage skill.

Example commentary shown for a position where opponent plays F5 (bad move): detectors identify the queen-trap threat and the Bishop G5 line, and commentary explains why capturing the center pawn defends against the threat.

Demo return: Claude Code is still processing, adds a comment investigating the position, and asks a clarifying question via Slack about what feels wrong; the presenters confirm the commentary was actually correct.
limitations: LLMs hallucinate when asked to play chess directly because they are trained on language, not calculation.
Gemini Flash still does not pass all 16 eval scenarios (~75% pass rate), so the team continuously tests new models.
Reasoning models provide good quality but have unpredictable latency, unsuitable for the instantaneous post-game phase.
Context extraction model development is initially a slow, painful process of building and pruning a large JSON structure.
High-effort Claude Code runs on reported commentary can take a while, so the demo continued on other slides while it processed.
LLMs still hallucinate even in the translator role, though grounding reduces it.
